term: can fail to be (Met. IX.8) / can be otherwise (Met. XII.7)
resolution: Both render ἐνδέχεται with a contrary state, and the Lambda.7 route to pure act passes from one to the other, so the passage is made explicit. CanFailToBe (IX.8, 1050b8-15; In Metaph. IX, lect. 9 n. 2-4) is read in the two-way sense of the potency of the contradictory: what is in potency to r is able to be r and able not to be r. CanBeOtherwise (XII.7, 1072b4-8; In Metaph. XII, lect. 7 n. 12-13) is the ability to be other than one is in r. The case keeps two primitives. STMT-EVERY-POTENCY-IS-OF-CONTRADICTION uses only CanFailToBe; STMT-SOME-UNMOVED-MOVER-CANNOT-BE-OTHERWISE and STMT-EVERY-UNMOVED-MOVER-CANNOT-BE-OTHERWISE use only CanBeOtherwise. The step between them is the explicit, unattributed bridge STMT-WHAT-CAN-FAIL-TO-BE-CAN-BE-OTHERWISE, which holds in the two-way sense and fails if 'can fail to be r' is read as the bare possibility of not being r (an unchangeable being that is not r would have it). No argument identifies the two predicates silently. The bare sense is not adopted anywhere in the case. In Metaph. XII, lect. 7 n. 13 does not supply the bridge: it infers (unde sequitur) from the mover's not being able to be otherwise that the first motion, a different subject, cannot not be, and n. 15 denies that this necessity is the absolute 'cannot be otherwise'; so it does not tie the two for one subject in one respect. Aristotle's 'ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἄρα ἐστὶν ὄν' (XII.7, 1072b10) is the closer witness and is queued with candidate ARIST-MET-V-5-NECESSARY-CANNOT-BE-OTHERWISE.
